lessons.title: Determining Optimal Harvest Time
lessons.body: Harvesting black soldier fly larvae at the right time gives you the best quality and quantity. If you harvest too early, larvae are small and yield is low. If you wait too long, larvae turn into pupae or even adult flies, and they stop eating. The ideal time to harvest is when larvae are in their fifth instar (the last stage before pupation). At this stage, they are about 2 cm long, plump, and light cream to pale yellow in colour. They have stopped feeding and are looking for a dry place to pupate. In warm African climates (25â30Â°C), this stage is reached about 14 to 18 days after the eggs hatch. In cooler conditions, it may take up to 21 days. Check your larvae every day after day 12. Look for larvae that are crawling out of the feeding substrate and moving towards the edges or up the walls of your bin. This is a clear sign they are ready. Another sign is that the substrate becomes more liquid and smells less like rotting food, because the larvae have consumed most of it. You can also use a simple sieve to check size: if most larvae are longer than your fingernail (about 1.5â2 cm), they are ready. Do not wait for all larvae to become black or dark brown; those are prepupae and are also good for harvest, but they have less fat. For maximum protein and fat, harvest when they are still white or cream. Plan to harvest in the morning when it is cooler, as larvae are less active. Use a shovel or gloved hands to scoop out a handful and inspect. If you see many small larvae still, wait 2â3 more days. If you see many dark, hard cases (pupae), you have waited too long. Regular observation is key. Keep a notebook to record the date you first saw larvae and the date you harvest, so you can predict future harvests. In Africa, where temperatures are often high, development is faster, so check earlier than you might expect.

lessons.title: Separating Larvae from Substrate
lessons.body: After harvesting, you need to separate the larvae from the remaining substrate (frass, uneaten food, and bedding). This can be done in several ways, depending on your scale. For small-scale farmers (a few kilograms per day), the simplest method is to use a sieve. Get a sieve with a mesh size of about 2â3 mm. Put a handful of the harvested mixture into the sieve and shake it gently over a bucket. The frass and small particles fall through, while the larvae remain on top. You may need to pick out any large lumps of substrate by hand. Another method is water flotation. Put the mixture in a bucket of water. The larvae will float, while the heavier frass and food particles sink. Skim the larvae off the top with a strainer or your hands. This method is fast but uses water, and the larvae become wet, so you must dry them quickly to prevent spoilage. For medium-scale farmers (10â50 kg per day), a mechanical shaker or a rotating drum sieve can save time. You can build a simple shaker using a wooden frame and a mesh screen, powered by hand or a small motor. For large-scale operations, commercial separators are available, but they are expensive. A low-cost option is to use a cement mixer with a mesh screen inside; as it rotates, the frass falls out and larvae stay in. After separation, the frass is a valuable fertiliser. You can sell it or use it on your farm. Do not throw it away. The larvae should be collected in a clean container. If you used water flotation, spread the larvae on a screen or cloth to drain and dry for 30 minutes before further processing. Always wear gloves and a mask when separating, as the dust from frass can be irritating. Work in a well-ventilated area. If you are separating by hand, it can take 1â2 hours for 10 kg of mixture. With practice, you will get faster. Remember to clean your equipment after each use to prevent disease and odours.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Killing Larvae
lessons.body: After separating larvae from substrate, they are still dirty and alive. You must clean and kill them quickly to prevent them from pupating or spoiling. Cleaning removes any remaining frass, bacteria, and dirt. Killing stops enzymatic activity that causes spoilage and makes them safe to process. Start by rinsing the larvae in clean water. Put them in a large bowl or bucket and add enough water to cover them. Stir gently with your hand or a spoon. The larvae will sink, and dirt will float. Pour off the dirty water and repeat 2â3 times until the water runs clear. Do not leave them in water for more than 10 minutes, as they can drown and become mushy. After rinsing, you need to kill them. The most common method is blanching: bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the larvae and boil for 2â3 minutes. This kills them instantly and also cleans them further. Do not overcook, or they become tough and lose nutrients. Another method is freezing: spread the larvae on a tray and put them in a freezer for at least 4 hours. Freezing is slower but preserves nutrients well. However, freezing requires electricity, which may not be available in rural areas. A third method is sun-drying: spread larvae thinly on a mat and dry under strong sun for 2â3 days. This kills them slowly and may allow some to escape. For most African farmers, boiling is the best because it is quick, cheap, and does not require electricity. After boiling, drain the larvae in a colander and spread them on a clean cloth or screen to cool and dry. You can now proceed to drying or milling. If you are not processing immediately, you can store the boiled larvae in a refrigerator for up to 2 days, but it is better to dry them. Always use clean water and clean utensils. Wash your hands before handling. The goal is to produce safe, high-quality larvae for animal feed.

lessons.title: Drying and Milling Larvae
lessons.body: Drying is the most important step to preserve larvae. If you do not dry them properly, they will rot or grow mould. The goal is to reduce moisture content to below 10%. There are three main drying methods: sun drying, oven drying, and solar drying. Sun drying is the cheapest and most common in Africa. Spread the boiled larvae in a thin layer (no more than 2 cm thick) on a clean mat, tray, or concrete floor. Place them in direct sunlight. Turn them every 2â3 hours to ensure even drying. Depending on the weather, it takes 2â4 days to dry completely. In humid conditions, it may take longer. To test if they are dry, take a few larvae and try to break them. They should be brittle and snap easily. If they are still soft or chewy, dry them longer. Oven drying is faster but requires electricity or gas. Set the oven to 60â70Â°C and spread larvae on a baking tray. Dry for 4â6 hours, stirring occasionally. Do not use high heat, as it destroys nutrients. Solar drying uses a solar dryer, which is a box with a glass top and ventilation holes. It reaches higher temperatures than open sun and protects from rain and insects. Drying takes 1â2 days. After drying, the larvae are crisp. You can store them whole or mill them into powder. Milling increases digestibility and makes it easier to mix with other feed ingredients. Use a hammer mill, a blender, or a mortar and pestle for small quantities. For medium scale, a diesel-powered hammer mill is ideal. Mill to a fine powder. Sieve the powder to remove any hard parts. The powder should be light brown and smell slightly nutty. Store in airtight containers. One kilogram of fresh larvae yields about 300â400 grams of dried larvae, and about 250â350 grams of powder. The powder is high in protein (40â45%) and fat (30â35%), making it excellent for poultry, pigs, and fish.

lessons.title: Storing Processed Larvae
lessons.body: Proper storage keeps your processed larvae safe and nutritious for months. After drying or milling, the larvae must be stored in airtight containers. Moisture is the enemy: if moisture gets in, mould will grow. Use clean, dry containers with tight-fitting lids. Plastic buckets with sealable lids, glass jars, or heavy-duty plastic bags are good. If using bags, squeeze out all air before sealing. Store in a cool, dark, dry place. A cupboard or a shelf away from sunlight is fine. Avoid storing near chemicals, fuel, or strong-smelling items, as the powder absorbs odours. The ideal storage temperature is below 25Â°C. In hot African climates, store in the coolest part of your house or in a root cellar. If you have a refrigerator, you can store powder there for up to 6 months. Without refrigeration, properly dried whole larvae can last 3â6 months, and powder can last 2â3 months. To extend shelf life, you can add natural antioxidants like rosemary extract or vitamin E, but this is optional. Always label your containers with the date of processing. Use older stock first. Check stored larvae every 2 weeks for signs of mould, insects, or off-smells. If you see clumping, it means moisture has entered; dry the product again in the sun or oven. If you see mould, discard the whole batch, as it can be toxic. For long-term storage, vacuum sealing is best but may be expensive. A simple alternative is to store in sealed buckets with a layer of desiccant (like silica gel) at the bottom, but ensure it does not touch the powder. Keep rodents and insects away by storing on high shelves or in metal drums. Sell or use your stored larvae within the recommended time. Remember, well-stored larvae are a valuable source of protein for your animals, especially during dry seasons when other feed is scarce.

lessons.title: Quality Control of Harvested Larvae
lessons.body: Quality control ensures your larvae are safe, nutritious, and free from contaminants. Start with the larvae themselves. They should be uniform in size and colour. Reject any that are dark, black, or have a foul smell. These may be dead or diseased. After harvesting, check for foreign objects like stones, plastic, or metal. Remove them by hand or with a sieve. During cleaning, use clean water. If the water is dirty, the larvae will be contaminated. After boiling, the larvae should be firm and white. If they are mushy, they were overcooked or not fresh. During drying, ensure they are completely dry. Moisture content above 10% leads to mould. You can test by putting a few dried larvae in a sealed jar for 24 hours. If condensation forms on the inside, they are not dry enough. After milling, check the powder for consistency. It should be fine and free of lumps. Sieve it to remove any hard pieces. The powder should have a pleasant, slightly nutty smell, not rancid or sour. Rancidity happens if the fat oxidises, which occurs when stored too long or exposed to air. To test for rancidity, smell the powder; if it smells like old oil, it is bad. You can also do a simple float test: put a spoon of powder in water. Good powder sinks slowly, while rancid powder floats due to released oils. For a more scientific approach, you can send a sample to a lab to test protein and fat content, but this is costly. For most farmers, sensory checks are enough. Keep records of each batch: date of harvest, date of processing, and any observations. This helps you trace problems. If you sell your larvae, buyers will ask for consistent quality. Always package in clean, labelled bags. Do not mix old and new batches. If you find a batch with mould or bad smell, do not sell it. Use it for compost or discard. Quality control is not just about rules; it is about pride in your product and the health of the animals you feed.

quiz.q: What is the ideal stage to harvest black soldier fly larvae for maximum protein and fat?
options: A) When they are newly hatched
B) When they are in the fifth instar (prepupae)
C) When they have turned into adult flies
D) When they are still eggs
quiz.explanation: Fifth instar larvae are fully grown and have the highest protein and fat content before pupation.

quiz.q: In warm African climates, how many days after hatching do larvae usually reach harvest size?
quiz.explanation: At 25â30Â°C, larvae develop quickly and are ready to harvest in about 14â18 days.

quiz.q: Which sign indicates that larvae are ready to harvest?
options: A) They are crawling out of the substrate
B) They are still very small
C) The substrate is dry and crumbly
D) They have turned into pupae
quiz.explanation: When larvae are ready to pupate, they leave the wet substrate in search of a dry place.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to check if larvae are large enough to harvest?
quiz.explanation: A sieve with 2â3 mm mesh helps separate larvae from frass and lets you inspect their size.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid waiting until all larvae are black or dark brown?
options: B) They have less fat and protein
quiz.explanation: Prepupae (dark) have already used some of their fat reserves, so white or cream larvae have higher nutritional value.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest larvae?
options: A) Midday when it is hottest
C) Morning when it is cooler
D) Any time, it doesn't matter
quiz.explanation: Larvae are less active in cooler morning temperatures, making them easier to handle.

quiz.q: Which method uses water to separate larvae from substrate?
quiz.explanation: In water flotation, larvae float while heavier frass sinks, allowing easy separation.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of water flotation?
options: B) It uses a lot of water and makes larvae wet
quiz.explanation: Water flotation uses water and leaves larvae wet, so they must be dried quickly to prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: What can you do with the frass after separating larvae?
quiz.explanation: Frass is a nutrient-rich organic fertiliser that can be sold or used on crops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mesh size for a sieve to separate larvae?
quiz.explanation: A 2â3 mm mesh allows frass to fall through while retaining larvae.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a mask when separating larvae from frass?
options: B) To prevent inhaling dust that can irritate lungs
C) To keep larvae out of your mouth
quiz.explanation: Frass dust can be irritating to the respiratory system, so a mask protects your health.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning harvested larvae?
quiz.explanation: Rinsing removes dirt, frass, and bacteria before killing the larvae.

quiz.q: How long should you boil larvae to kill them?
quiz.explanation: Boiling for 2â3 minutes kills larvae quickly without overcooking them.

quiz.q: Which killing method requires electricity?
quiz.explanation: Freezing requires a freezer, which needs electricity, unlike boiling or sun-drying.

quiz.q: What happens if you overcook larvae during boiling?
options: B) They become tough and lose nutrients
quiz.explanation: Overcooking makes larvae tough and can destroy some heat-sensitive nutrients.

quiz.q: After boiling, what should you do before drying?
options: B) Drain and spread to cool
quiz.explanation: Draining and cooling prevents excess moisture and prepares larvae for drying.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for dried larvae?
quiz.explanation: Moisture below 10% inhibits mould and bacterial growth, ensuring long shelf life.

quiz.q: Which drying method is cheapest and most common in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sun drying uses free sunlight and requires no special equipment.

quiz.q: How can you test if larvae are completely dry?
options: A) They are soft and chewy
B) They are brittle and snap easily
quiz.explanation: Dry larvae should be brittle; if they bend, they still contain moisture.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of milling dried larvae into powder?
options: B) It makes it easier to mix with other feeds
quiz.explanation: Powder mixes evenly with other ingredients, improving feed formulation.

quiz.q: Approximately how much dried larvae do you get from 1 kg of fresh larvae?
quiz.explanation: Fresh larvae are about 70% water, so 1 kg yields roughly 300â400 g of dried product.

quiz.q: What is the typical protein content of dried black soldier fly larvae?
quiz.explanation: Dried BSF larvae are rich in protein, containing about 40â45%.

quiz.q: Why should you store processed larvae in airtight containers?
options: B) To prevent moisture and mould
C) To keep the smell in
D) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers block moisture, which is the main cause of spoilage.

quiz.q: Where is the best place to store processed larvae?
options: B) In a cool, dark, dry place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dark, dry conditions slow down oxidation and prevent mould growth.

quiz.q: How long can properly dried whole larvae last without refrigeration?
quiz.explanation: With good drying and storage, whole larvae can last 3â6 months.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould in stored larvae?
options: A) Scrape it off and use the rest
B) Dry it again in the sun
D) Feed it to animals anyway
quiz.explanation: Mould can produce toxins that are harmful to animals, so the entire batch should be discarded.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label stored larvae with the processing date?
options: A) To know when to sell
B) To use older stock first
quiz.explanation: First-in, first-out (FIFO) rotation ensures older stock is used before it spoils.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor quality dried larvae?
quiz.explanation: Rancid or sour smell indicates fat oxidation or spoilage, meaning poor quality.

quiz.q: What simple test can indicate if powder is rancid?
quiz.explanation: Rancid powder smells like old oil; a smell test is quick and reliable.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of each batch of processed larvae?
options: A) To trace problems and ensure consistency
quiz.explanation: Records help identify issues and maintain quality control across batches.
